  ([convert to your time zone](https://www.timeanddate.com/worldclock/converter.html?iso=20261012T110000&p1=230&p2=179&p3=248))
- First meeting: 2026-10-12. Facilitator: Ángel Féliz
- 1 introduction session + 14 chapters, each with **one session for the chapter and one for its exercises**
- Planned to finish in April 2027
- Full calendar: [sign-up sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1u7XiaM3OyQe-EkYdBJ0WO8-E9Iv8goq-pvy9ouWJ4Sk/edit?usp=sharing)

## What a meeting looks like

-   A volunteer leads the discussion of a chapter in one hour
    -   **This is the best way to learn the material.**
-   The presentation covers:
    -   The main ideas of the chapter
    -   Questions you have
    -   Maybe a live demo
-   **You don't need to be an expert.** If something wasn't clear, bring it up and we figure it out together
-   Chapter too long for one hour? We split it and continue the following week

## Exercises

- Each chapter ends with review, problem-solving and programming questions
- Pick what suits you:
  - Solve the exercises in the book
  - Apply the concepts in code, with the book's Python modules or an external dataset
- The book text has no code listings, so implementing things takes some extra research. With coding experience and an LLM for guidance you can get far
- Depending on the group's interest, a chapter can get up to **two weeks** of exercises and coding

## Can't attend live?

- Every meeting is recorded: [DSLC YouTube channel (DSLC.video)](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLLQZd6pMgcUA)
- All slide decks: [GitHub Pages](https://AngelFelizR.github.io/bookclub-sdamodeling)
- Ask questions, share materials and post your thoughts in Slack at any time
- **You can learn with us asynchronously.** Missing sessions is fine

# About the book

## The book at a glance {.smaller}

- *Sequential Decision Analytics and Modeling (2e)*, Warren B. Powell (February 2026), subtitle: *Modeling with Python*
- Sequential decision problems always look like this:

  *decision, information, decision, information, decision, ...*

- Each decision brings a cost or reward, and decisions are made with a method called a **policy**
- Central goal: design policies that work well over time, under uncertainty about information that has not arrived yet
- Examples are "the mathematics of everyday life": selling an asset, inventories, routes, drug testing, ads, supply chains
- Goal: learn **how to think** about these problems, even if you never write a line of code

## Who is it for? {.smaller}

- Aimed at undergraduate or master's students who have taken **a course in probability and statistics**
- No linear programming needed (one example, blood management, uses it)
- Teach-by-example style: every chapter is built around a specific problem
- Chapters 2-6 and 8-14 follow the same outline, so they can be read in any order
- Optional reference for more depth: Powell's graduate text *Reinforcement Learning and Stochastic Optimization* ([tinyurl.com/RLandSO](https://tinyurl.com/RLandSO/))

## How the book is organized {.smaller}

| Part | Chapters | What happens |
|------|----------|--------------|
| Universal Modeling Framework | 1 | Light overview of the framework using two inventory problems |
| Simple examples | 2-6 | One problem per chapter, chosen to bring out the four classes of policies |
| Universal Modeling Framework | 7 | Returns to the framework in more depth, using chapters 2-6 as context |
| Complex examples | 8-14 | Richer settings: uncertainty modeling, multiple agents, more advanced policies |

Our **Chapter 0** is the club's own introduction (this deck).

## The two big ideas (Chapter 1) {.smaller}

**Five elements of every sequential decision model**

1. State variables $S_t$ (physical, information and belief state)
2. Decision variables $x_t$
3. Exogenous information $W_{t+1}$
4. Transition function $S^M(S_t, x_t, W_{t+1})$
5. Objective function

**Four classes of policies** (they cover any method for making decisions)

- *Policy search:* **PFA** (policy function approximations), **CFA** (cost function approximations)
- *Lookahead:* **VFA** (value function approximations), **DLA** (direct lookahead approximations)

## Chapters 2-6: simple examples {.smaller}

| Ch | Problem | Main idea |
|----|---------|-----------|
| 2 | Asset selling | Optimal stopping; simple tunable policies |
| 3 | Adaptive market planning | Newsvendor; stochastic gradient, where the stepsize is the decision |
| 4 | Learning the best diabetes medication | Learning with beliefs; bandit problems |
| 5 | Stochastic shortest path (static) | Bellman's equation and approximate dynamic programming |
| 6 | Stochastic shortest path (dynamic) | Deterministic lookahead made better with tunable parameters |

## Chapters 7-14: going further {.smaller}

| Ch | Problem | Main idea |
|----|---------|-----------|
| 7 | Applications, revisited | Four policy classes in depth, types of state variables, online vs. offline objectives |
| 8 | Energy storage I | Models for electricity prices; buy-low-sell-high and approximate DP |
| 9 | Energy storage II | Changing wind forecasts; Gaussian processes and hidden-state models |
| 10 | Supply chain I: two-agent newsvendor | Introduction to multiagent problems |
| 11 | Supply chain II: the beer game | Multiple agents, anchor-and-adjustment heuristic |
| 12 | Ad-click optimization | Bidding under three kinds of uncertainty; knowledge gradient |
| 13 | Blood management | Multidimensional resource allocation; linear programming and VFAs |
| 14 | Optimizing clinical trials | Three direct lookahead policies of growing sophistication |

## Exercises and companion Python code {.smaller}

- Each chapter closes with three kinds of exercises:
  - **Review questions:** reinforce the basics
  - **Problem-solving questions:** modeling challenges
  - **Programming questions:** use the book's Python modules, sometimes modifying the code
- The library (rewritten for Python 3 by Prof. Dennis Djanka, including Jupyter notebooks for some problems) is at [tinyurl.com/sdagithub](https://tinyurl.com/sdagithub/)
- Modules named in the exercises: AssetSelling (ch. 2), AdaptiveMarketPlanning (ch. 3), StochasticShortestPath Static and Dynamic (ch. 5-6), EnergyStorage I (ch. 8), TwoNewsvendor (ch. 10), BloodManagement (ch. 13), ClinicalTrials (ch. 14)
- Also useful: [supplementary material](https://tinyurl.com/sdamodelingsupplements/) and Powell's [undergraduate course slides](https://tinyurl.com/RLSOcourses/) for this book

::: notes
Chapters 1, 7, 9, 11 and 12 do not name a Python module in their exercises. Chapter 4's programming exercises name AdaptiveMarketPlanning in the text, which looks like a copy-paste slip (the preface lists a diabetes module). Check the repository for exact file names.
:::

## What is new in the 2nd edition

- Chapter 1 now discusses different **types of decisions**
- Every application chapter starts with a **Chapter overview**
- New **Framing the problem** section after each narrative: performance metrics, decisions and sources of uncertainty, described in plain English before any math
- Proofreading throughout; same set of application chapters
- Published through Kindle Direct Publishing (Kindle and hardbound editions)

# How to present

## Want to present a chapter?

1. Open the [Cohort 1 sign-up sheet](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1u7XiaM3OyQe-EkYdBJ0WO8-E9Iv8goq-pvy9ouWJ4Sk/edit?usp=sharing) (also pinned in Slack)
2. Put your name next to a chapter and date
3. Prepare your slides (next slides explain how)

*Presenting is how you learn. Ángel is happy to help you through the process.*

## Overview: slides are code

- Every deck is a `.qmd` file in `slides/` (`slides/03.qmd` = chapter 3)
- The site is a Quarto website, hosted on GitHub
- Your slides reach the site through a **pull request (PR)**
- Once the PR is merged, the site rebuilds automatically

Full instructions: [the GitHub repo README](https://github.com/AngelFelizR/bookclub-sdamodeling)

## One-time setup

1. Install git and an editor (RStudio/Positron for R, VS Code for Python)
2. Fork and clone the repo
    - R: `usethis::create_from_github("AngelFelizR/bookclub-sdamodeling")`
    - git: click **Fork** on GitHub, then `git clone`
3. Install R packages with `pak::pak()`
    - **Required even for Python slides**: Quarto runs an R script before every render
4. Python slides only: install Python 3.11+, then `pip install jupyter ipykernel` and `pip install .`

## Each time you present

1. **Create a branch** (`usethis::pr_init("chapter-3")` or `git switch -c chapter-3`)
2. **Edit** `slides/NN.qmd` (`#` = section, `##` = slide)
3. **Add the packages** you used
4. **Preview**: `Ctrl/Cmd-Shift-K` or `quarto preview slides/NN.qmd`
5. **Commit** your changes
6. **Push and open a PR** (`usethis::pr_push()` or `git push -u origin chapter-3`)
7. **After merge**, clean up (`usethis::pr_finish()` or delete the branch)

## R or Python?

- **R:** no special header; add packages with `usethis::use_package("pkg")`
- **Python:** start the file with `engine: jupyter`; list packages in `pyproject.toml`
- You can mix: the engine is chosen per file
- The book's own code is in Python, but your slides can use either language

## Ground rules

- `main` is protected: **nobody pushes directly**, everything goes through a PR
- A PR must pass its automated checks before merging
- Stuck? Ask in Slack

## Learning objectives (LOs)

-   Students who study with LOs in mind ***retain more***
-   **Tips:**
    -   Think "After today's session, you will be able to {LO}"
    -   *Very* roughly **1 per heading**

# Club logistics

## Pace

-   **Goal:** 1 chapter / 2 weeks (chapter session + exercises session)
-   OK to split overwhelming chapters
-   OK to combine short chapters
-   Meet ***every*** week except holidays, etc.
-   Slack is a good place for offline discussion and troubleshooting

## Group introductions

- If you feel comfortable sharing:
  - Who are you?
  - What do you do?
  - What is your background?
  - How long have you been using R/Python?
  - What are you most looking forward to during the club?
  - What do you expect to get from this book?
